raw_graphql_pull_request.body:
## Purpose
Fixes #60685.

EPLB records load per physical expert. When step_interval < window_size, part of the window still holds load recorded under the old map, and the next rearrange counts it for the expert that now sits at that physical index.

This PR records load by logical expert instead. `_eplb_map_and_record_i32_kernel` already has the logical id, so the `atomic_add` now goes to the logical id rather than the physical index. `expert_load_pass` and the window have logical width, so old steps stay with the right expert after the map changes, and rearrange only sums the window. No extra kernel or scatter is added.

The PR also removes `expert_load_pass_buffer`, `last_expert_load` and `use_last_expert_load`. The number of logical experts does not change when Elastic EP scales, so the window stays valid across a scale and the scale rearrange uses it directly. `log_balancedness` now splits each logical expert's load evenly over its replicas, which is an estimate of the per physical expert load.

No open PR fixes this. #49700 only clears the window on an elastic EP topology change.

## Test Plan
- `pytest tests/kernels/moe/test_routing.py tests/distributed/test_eplb_utils.py` on H100
- Atomic contention microbench of the record kernel on H100, main vs this PR, CUDA graph of 100 calls, median of 20, top_k 8, extra replicas on the 8 hottest experts. "hot" sends half of all picks to one expert.
- gsm8k on 2xH100: DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat, TP 2, EP + EPLB async, `window_size=1000, step_interval=100, num_redundant_experts=2`, 5-shot, 2 runs per side.
- `pytest tests/distributed/test_elastic_ep.py -k "enforce_eager_heavy or cuda_graphs_heavy"` on 4xH100, main vs this PR. This scales dp 2 to 4 and back under heavy traffic and checks gsm8k after each scale.

## Test Result
`test_routing.py` + `test_eplb_utils.py`: 513 passed. The changed routing tests and the new `test_log_balancedness_from_logical_load` fail on main as expected.

Record kernel time per call (us):

| model | dist | tokens | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 256+32 experts | uniform | 1024 | 4.28 | 4.33 |
| 256+32 experts | uniform | 16384 | 34.92 | 35.98 |
| 256+32 experts | zipf | 16384 | 37.62 | 38.31 |
| 256+32 experts | hot | 1024 | 4.22 | 4.76 |
| 256+32 experts | hot | 16384 | 33.85 | 43.43 |
| 128+32 experts | uniform | 16384 | 40.57 | 26.97 |
| 128+32 experts | hot | 16384 | 40.39 | 33.85 |

Uniform and zipf are within noise. With one very hot expert out of 256, recording on the logical id costs up to about 10 us per layer at 16k tokens and under 1 us at 1k tokens. The 128+32 case got faster. Both runs gave the same numbers.

gsm8k accuracy:

| | run 1 | run 2 |
|---|---|---|
| main | 0.6368 | 0.6323 |
| this PR | 0.6399 | 0.6384 |

Every run did 19 async rearranges with no errors.

Elastic EP scaling: 3 passed on main and 3 passed on this PR (`enforce_eager_heavy`, `cuda_graphs_heavy`, `cuda_graphs_heavy_nixl_ep`). gsm8k on 256 questions:

| case | | initial | after 2 to 4 |
|---|---|---|---|
| enforce_eager_heavy | main | 0.688 | 0.676 |
| enforce_eager_heavy | this PR | 0.660 | 0.664 |
| cuda_graphs_heavy | main | 0.645 | 0.652 |
| cuda_graphs_heavy | this PR | 0.648 | 0.656 |
| cuda_graphs_heavy_nixl_ep | main | 0.645 | 0.664 |
| cuda_graphs_heavy_nixl_ep | this PR | 0.676 | 0.664 |

The test also checks accuracy after scaling back to 2, and that check passed in every case.

nodes.body:
Thanks @itayalroy it makes sense. What do you think about doing the logical conversion once per step instead of in the forward pass?

I mean leaving the forward pass as is so it keeps counting per physical slot in `expert_load_pass`. Then, in `step()` when the `expert_load_pass` is copied into `expert_load_window` we can apply`scatter_add_` by the logical ID using the `physical_to_logical_map` so the window will hold load per logical expert. The scatter index is cached and rebuilt only when the map changes.

I think this is safer than counting by logical ID in the forward pass, since recording code stays untouched, including the code that lives in `_eplb_map_and_record_i32_kernel` in `base_router.py` and also in model specific paths like deepseek_v4 and kimi_k3 that would otherwise need to change. `log_balancedness` also needs the per-physical counts to compute load per rank, and this keeps them. The extra work runs once per step for all layers together and not once per layer per forward. It solves both of your points because the copy happens before any commit. Nothing has to be cleared when the map changes.

I measured it on 4xH100 with DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat and EP with rearranges every 200 steps. The per-step copy went from about 9.2us to 10.5us, rearrange() got about 2x faster because the window is already logical, and E2E throughput was 80.3 req/s on main vs 81.3 with this change over 6 runs each. Already updated the PR with this, but happy to change it if you prefer a different approach

The per-step copy went from about 9.2us to 10.5us, rearrange() got about 2x faster because the window is already logical, and E2E throughput was 80.3 req/s on main vs 81.3 with this change over 6 runs each. Already updated the PR with this, but happy to change it if you prefer a different approach

I benchmarked this PR with DeepSeek V4 Pro on 20 GB200 GPUs. Compared with upstream, the median gap between forward passes (measured with CUDA events immediately after one forward call and before the next) increased by about 11 µs, and the EPLB step itself increased by the same amount. No measurable effect on e2e performance though.

I suspect the extra kernel launch accounts for much of that 11 µs. A fused Triton kernel would probably help here (it could even improve performance over upstream as we can fuse three kernels into one, compared with two kernel launches in upstream), but it would add code complexity, so not sure if it is worth it.

@tlrmchlsmth @ilmarkov for vis

Thank you for the fix, it does make sense!

Regarding adding extra torch calls on the hot path.
Could we record logical-expert load in the existing `_eplb_map_and_record_i32_kernel`? It already has the logical expert_id before selecting physical_id, so this could let step() copy the counts into the window and avoid the new per-step `zero_().scatter_add_` and cached index.
Physical counts are still needed for optional `log_balancedness`; we could keep physical recording for that mode. The tradeoff to benchmark is atomic contention when several replicas of a popular logical expert share one counter.
Also, could you please add accuracy validation results (e.g. `gsm8k`)?
@ilmarkov yes I'll do that even though I don't see any signal for accuracy being affected. I'll soon look into your suggestion as well thanks

I moved the recording into `_eplb_map_and_record_i32_kernel` so it counts by logical id, and I dropped the step() scatter. This also removes the extra launch from the forward gap.

Results on H100:
- gsm8k on DeepSeek-V2-Lite, TP 2, EP + async EPLB, 2 runs per side: main 0.6368 / 0.6323, PR 0.6399 / 0.6384. Each run did 19 rearranges with no errors.
- Atomic contention on the record kernel: uniform and zipf routing are within noise. With one very hot expert out of 256 it costs up to about 10 us per layer at 16k tokens and under 1 us at 1k tokens.
- `test_elastic_ep.py` (eager, CUDA graphs and nixl_ep, heavy traffic) passes on 4xH100. The scale rearrange now uses the logical window instead of `last_expert_load`.

The full tables are in the description.

## Claude Code Review

This pull request is from a fork — automated review is disabled. A repository maintainer can comment `@claude review` to run a one-time review.

This is a real issue with our current EPLB implementation (I mentioned it in #58473’s description as well), but I see two problems with this fix:

1. This is dangerous for async EPLB. Async EPLB transfers one layer at a time, so `_commit_eplb_maps_for_layer()` for the last layers might happen very close to the next EPLB reshuffle, depending on transfer time and window/step configs. That reshuffle could use very little data for those layers, or even no data if the last layer is committed in the same step that triggers a reshuffle. This can result in really bad mappings which severely hurt e2e performance.

2. For sync EPLB, this change effectively silently sets window_size to step_interval whenever window_size > step_interval, which is pretty misleading

I spent some time thinking about this while fixing #58473. I think the safest solution is to record load by logical expert, so changing the physical mapping does not invalidate the history. But this is not an easy change as we need to make sure we do it without slowing down statistics collection.
Also note that if we record expert load by logical expert, we don't need this EEP w/a anymore, we can remove it and clean up some code

We should use actual physical-expert counts for log_balancedness. We should record both logical and physical expert load in the existing routing kernel when log_balancedness is enabled.

Logical counts keep the rearrangement window valid across map changes, physical counts let us report actual per-rank balance. Splitting logical load evenly among replicas can hide a skewed replica and make balancedness look better than it is.

Thanks @itayalroy it makes sense. What do you think about doing the logical conversion once per step instead of in the forward pass?

I mean leaving the forward pass as is so it keeps counting per physical slot in `expert_load_pass`. Then, in `step()` when the `expert_load_pass` is copied into `expert_load_window` we can apply`scatter_add_` by the logical ID using the `physical_to_logical_map` so the window will hold load per logical expert. The scatter index is cached and rebuilt only when the map changes.

I think this is safer than counting by logical ID in the forward pass, since recording code stays untouched, including the code that lives in `_eplb_map_and_record_i32_kernel` in `base_router.py` and also in model specific paths like deepseek_v4 and kimi_k3 that would otherwise need to change. `log_balancedness` also needs the per-physical counts to compute load per rank, and this keeps them. The extra work runs once per step for all layers together and not once per layer per forward. It solves both of your points because the copy happens before any commit. Nothing has to be cleared when the map changes.

I measured it on 4xH100 with DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat and EP with rearranges every 200 steps. The per-step copy went from about 9.2us to 10.5us, rearrange() got about 2x faster because the window is already logical, and E2E throughput was 80.3 req/s on main vs 81.3 with this change over 6 runs each. Already updated the PR with this, but happy to change it if you prefer a different approach

I benchmarked this PR with DeepSeek V4 Pro on 20 GB200 GPUs. Compared with upstream, the median gap between forward passes (measured with CUDA events immediately after one forward call and before the next) increased by about 11 µs, and the EPLB step itself increased by the same amount. No measurable effect on e2e performance though.

I suspect the extra kernel launch accounts for much of that 11 µs. A fused Triton kernel would probably help here (it could even improve performance over upstream as we can fuse three kernels into one, compared with two kernel launches in upstream), but it would add code complexity, so not sure if it is worth it.

@tlrmchlsmth @ilmarkov for vis

Thank you for the fix, it does make sense!

Regarding adding extra torch calls on the hot path.
Could we record logical-expert load in the existing `_eplb_map_and_record_i32_kernel`? It already has the logical expert_id before selecting physical_id, so this could let step() copy the counts into the window and avoid the new per-step `zero_().scatter_add_` and cached index.
Physical counts are still needed for optional `log_balancedness`; we could keep physical recording for that mode. The tradeoff to benchmark is atomic contention when several replicas of a popular logical expert share one counter.
Also, could you please add accuracy validation results (e.g. `gsm8k`)?
@ilmarkov yes I'll do that even though I don't see any signal for accuracy being affected. I'll soon look into your suggestion as well thanks

I moved the recording into `_eplb_map_and_record_i32_kernel` so it counts by logical id, and I dropped the step() scatter. This also removes the extra launch from the forward gap.

Results on H100:
- gsm8k on DeepSeek-V2-Lite, TP 2, EP + async EPLB, 2 runs per side: main 0.6368 / 0.6323, PR 0.6399 / 0.6384. Each run did 19 rearranges with no errors.
- Atomic contention on the record kernel: uniform and zipf routing are within noise. With one very hot expert out of 256 it costs up to about 10 us per layer at 16k tokens and under 1 us at 1k tokens.
- `test_elastic_ep.py` (eager, CUDA graphs and nixl_ep, heavy traffic) passes on 4xH100. The scale rearrange now uses the logical window instead of `last_expert_load`.

## Claude Code Review

This pull request is from a fork — automated review is disabled. A repository maintainer can comment `@claude review` to run a one-time review.

This is a real issue with our current EPLB implementation (I mentioned it in #58473’s description as well), but I see two problems with this fix:

1. This is dangerous for async EPLB. Async EPLB transfers one layer at a time, so `_commit_eplb_maps_for_layer()` for the last layers might happen very close to the next EPLB reshuffle, depending on transfer time and window/step configs. That reshuffle could use very little data for those layers, or even no data if the last layer is committed in the same step that triggers a reshuffle. This can result in really bad mappings which severely hurt e2e performance.

2. For sync EPLB, this change effectively silently sets window_size to step_interval whenever window_size > step_interval, which is pretty misleading

I spent some time thinking about this while fixing #58473. I think the safest solution is to record load by logical expert, so changing the physical mapping does not invalidate the history. But this is not an easy change as we need to make sure we do it without slowing down statistics collection.
